title: What the long story teaches
hook: faith kept through exile, loss and renewal

segments.voice: Yesterday, the kitchen at Amritsar, and your line was tens of thousands fed. Did you serve someone first, or wash a plate that wasn't yours? Today, we step back from the kitchen and look at the whole year's road. Day one thousand forty-four.

Stand at the end of a long road and look back, and you can't see every step. You see the shape. A man with a musician beside him, walking from village to village. Towns built around a pool and a kitchen. Gurus who gave their lives rather than give way. A morning when five stood up. Hard years in the hills and forests. A kingdom won and lost. Marches with no weapons. A land split in two. A temple attacked, and grief in the streets. Families scattered across oceans, building gurdwaras in rented halls. All year, this path has walked that road. Today, what the long story teaches.
screen: `A MAN AND A MUSICIAN, WALKING.` → `MARTYRS, MARCHES, A LAND SPLIT.` → `GURDWARAS IN RENTED HALLS.`

segments.voice: First, the losses are real. This story doesn't pretend. There were Gurus tortured and killed, families driven from their homes, sacred places damaged, and friends who never came back. Sikhs don't hide those names. They say them out loud. Second, the remembering. In the Ardas, the prayer said standing at the close of Sikh services, the sangat recalls those who gave their lives and kept their faith: who were cut limb from limb, broken on wheels, sawn apart, and who kept their Sikhi with their uncut hair to the last breath. The losses are not forgotten. They're carried, standing, every day. Third, the renewal. After every hard chapter, something kept going. The Granth kept being read. The kitchen kept cooking. The gurdwara door kept opening, in a village in Punjab, a river town in Malaysia, a rented hall in a northern winter. Sikhs often tell it this way: the faith didn't go on by winning every fight, but by keeping its daily practices. Fourth, the spirit. The Ardas ends with this line: Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhane sarbat da bhala. Through the Name, rising spirits, and by your will, the good of all. Chardi kala is the word for that spirit: rising, steady, even in loss. And notice what it asks for at the very end. Not victory. The good of all. That's today's line: the lesson of the story. As the Ardas holds it: remember everything, keep the practice, and keep asking good for everyone.
screen: `THE LOSSES ARE REAL.` · `THE ARDAS REMEMBERS THEM.` · `THE KITCHEN KEPT COOKING.` · `CHARDI KALA, AND THE GOOD OF ALL.` · then, large: `THE LESSON OF THE STORY.`

segments.voice: Two minutes for the whole road. Sit, and let your breath slow. Let the year's stories pass in front of you like a slow train: the musician, the five, the marches, the kitchens. Don't hold any of them. Let one stop in front of you, the one that stayed with you most. Breathe in, and look at it. Breathe out, and name, quietly, one thing it taught you. Only one. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
What the long story teaches. A faith kept through exile, loss and renewal: remembering the losses, keeping the daily practice, and asking, in chardi kala, for the good of all. Today's word.
screen: `WHAT THE LONG STORY TEACHES — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the lesson of the story. Today, write down the one lesson you named in the sit, in a single sentence, and put it somewhere you'll see it tomorrow. Day one thousand forty-four.

howItsDone: In the Ardas, said standing at the close of Sikh services and at other moments, the sangat remembers the Gurus and the Sikhs who gave their lives for their faith, and ends by asking for chardi kala through the Name and the good of all.

fork.setup: after a terrible loss, the sangat gathers to say the Ardas. at the end, what does it ask for?
options: revenge on those who did it.
rising spirits through the Name, and the good of all.
fork.reveal: nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhane sarbat da bhala. the losses are remembered, and the prayer still asks good for everyone.

original.note: chardi kala, rising spirits: the steady, hopeful spirit the Ardas asks for through the Name.

trapdoor: what you thought: a history summary.
what it means: a faith kept through exile, loss and renewal by remembering, practicing and hoping.
what a scholar hears: the Ardas holds both ends: it names the martyrs, then closes with chardi kala and sarbat da bhala, the good of all.

notes: Year-three look-back. The hook lists the year's arc in general terms with no dates or names; the lines 'a temple attacked, and grief in the streets' refer to 1984 without naming it. Please check the wording is respectful and adequate.

Editor pass: the Ardas remembrance paraphrase now follows the Ardas text (cut limb from limb, broken on wheels, sawn apart, kept Sikhi with uncut hair to the last breath) instead of 'burned', which the Ardas does not say in those words; 'survived ... when everything else was taken' softened to 'went on by keeping its daily practices'.

Audit pass: the narrator's own verdict on why the faith survived, and the closing imperative, now attributed to how Sikhs tell it and to the Ardas, so the narrator doesn't state a historical cause or instruct the listener.
